defects.title: P2P handshake fully trusts the server: an active server can fetch or swap any clip
defects.claim: The share offer relayed through the friends server carries everything needed to download: `Signal::ShareOffer { id, size, sha256, secret, addr, meta }`. The sender lets in anyone holding the secret, before any answer: `let open = matches!(entry.transfer.stage, Stage::Asking | Stage::Moving); if !same(entry.secret…) || !open` (comment: "Dialling in is their yes"). It never checks `connection.remote_id()`. iroh keys are new every run (`Endpoint::bind(presets::N0)`), so nothing can be pinned. The server sees every relay body (secret, sha256, sender address), so it can download or MITM the transfer. This breaks the privacy page's "never reaches our server" / end-to-end claim against anything other than a passive server.
defects.scenario: Needs the server operator, or whoever compromises the Worker or Cloudflare account. While the offer is in its 60 s Asking window, the server dials the sender and downloads the clip without the friend ever accepting. Or it replaces `addr` and `sha256` with its own endpoint and hash; the friend then receives the server's content, filed as "from <friend>", and the hash check passes.
defects.fix: Keep a persistent iroh secret key per install, protected with DPAPI. The receiver puts its NodeId in `ShareAnswer`; the sender serves only after an accepting answer and only to that `remote_id()`. Pin each friend's NodeId on first use and warn when it changes; optionally show a short safety code. Reword the privacy page.

defects.title: Size overflow in the offer lets a friend show "1.0 MB" and fill the disk; no size cap or free-space check on receive
defects.claim: `let total = size + meta.tracks.iter().map(|track| track.size).sum::<u64>();` — the release profile has no `overflow-checks`, so this wraps. With `size` = 1 MiB and `tracks[0].size` = 2^64-1 the banner shows "1.0 MB". After accept, `fetch_tracks` asks for track 0, the sender answers `rest` = 2^64-1, which passes the `offset + rest != size` check, and the receiver writes `…\tracks\<id>\0.m4a.part` until C: is full. Even without the overflow trick there is no upper limit on size and no free-space check anywhere in `receive`, unlike the 2 GB guard recordings have.
defects.scenario: An accepted friend sends a crafted offer (size 1 MiB, track size 2^64-1); the user clicks accept on a "1.0 MB" clip; the receiver writes until the disk is full. The recorder and the OS suffer before the 6 retries give up and the folder is deleted.
defects.fix: Use `checked_add` throughout. Reject offers above a sane cap (e.g. clip <= 64 GiB, each track <= 2 GiB, `track.size` <= `size`). Check free space on both volumes with `disk.rs` before accepting and while writing. Never write past `size`.

defects.title: An accepted friend can spam offers: banner, sound and toast each time, plus a slow UI
defects.claim: Every incoming offer inserts a map entry (an existing id is silently overwritten), plays `ClipReceived`, shows an overlay banner over the game and raises `Alert::Clip`, which is always wanted. The default is `accept_clips: AcceptClips::All`. The server's rate budget (30 messages per 10 s) is per WebSocket and is lost when the Durable Object hibernates, and a user may open any number of sockets, so the rate is effectively unbounded. Each `emit()` sends the whole transfer list to three webviews, so cost grows roughly with the square of the number of live offers (entries stay about 60 s or more).
defects.scenario: A friend scripts N sockets and floods offers during a match; the victim gets repeated banners/sounds/toasts and a slowing UI. The only remedies are blocking the friend or changing settings. Confirmed in code; size of the slowdown is likely, not measured.
defects.fix: Client side: at most 1-2 pending offers per friend and about 10 in total; reject ids that are already known (incoming or outgoing); one banner and one sound per friend per 30 s. Server side: a persisted per-user budget and a cap on sockets per user.

defects.title: An incomplete ffmpeg folder blocks setup for good, re-downloads every 30 minutes, and silently falls back to PATH ffmpeg
defects.claim: Setup does `if PROGRAMS.iter().all(|(name, _)| target.join(name).is_file()) { return Ok(()) }`, otherwise it downloads, then `std::fs::rename(&staging, target)`. If `9.0.1\` exists but `ffmpeg.exe` is gone (antivirus quarantine is a common false positive, or the user deleted it), the rename onto the existing non-empty folder fails on Windows with "could not put ffmpeg in place". It retries every 30 minutes forever, pulling the full archive each time. Meanwhile `tool()` quietly falls back to `PathBuf::from("ffmpeg")` (app folder or PATH), an untested and possibly old ffmpeg that then also parses friends' files.
defects.scenario: Antivirus quarantines `%LOCALAPPDATA%\gg.clippiboy.app\ffmpeg\9.0.1\ffmpeg.exe`; every 30 minutes the app downloads the whole archive and fails the rename; all ffmpeg work runs on whatever `ffmpeg` is on PATH.
defects.fix: When the folder is incomplete, `remove_dir_all(target)` before the rename (or unpack under a fresh name); don't fall back to PATH silently; keep the 30-minute retry from becoming a download loop.

defects.title: Files from friends go to ffmpeg unchecked, with format auto-detection, no whitelists, no timeout, on an async worker
defects.claim: The thumbnail for a received clip is made with `ffmpeg -ss 0.5 -i <received file> …`, and `file_clip` runs it synchronously inside the tokio task. Unlike the share-link server (`Mp4Boxes`), the P2P path never checks that the file is an MP4; ffmpeg picks the demuxer from the content. The pinned build's HLS demuxer refuses an `.mp4` name and concat runs with `safe=1`, which limits the obvious tricks, but ffmpeg parser bugs, playlist-style demuxers (DASH, concat reading sibling files) and any old PATH ffmpeg (NW-4) remain. `muxer::run` has no timeout/kill.
defects.scenario: A malicious friend sends a crafted file with a non-MP4 container; after accept, ffmpeg auto-detects and parses it (attack surface confirmed; exploitability speculative); a hanging ffmpeg also blocks the tokio worker indefinitely.
defects.fix: For received files add input options `-format_whitelist mov,mp4,m4a,3gp,3g2,mj2,matroska,webm,image2,png_pipe,jpeg_pipe -protocol_whitelist file` (and to every later ffmpeg/ffprobe input of such files), or check the box structure as the server does. Put a timeout and kill on `muxer::run`. Run `file_clip` in `spawn_blocking`.

defects.title: Two concurrent receives with the same file name share one .part file; duplicate offer ids can be accepted twice
defects.claim: `free_name` only checks the final name, so two concurrent transfers both get `X.mp4.part`. The second takes its resume offset from the first one's partly written file and truncates it (`set_len`). Rust opens files with `FILE_SHARE_DELETE`, so after the first renames the file into place, the second keeps writing into the clip that was already verified and filed. `rename` also replaces anything that appeared at the target since, and `free_name` hands back the existing target after 999 name collisions. An offer re-sent with the same id overwrites an entry that is already Moving and puts it back to Asking, so it can be accepted twice.
defects.scenario: The same clip is offered twice and both are accepted, or a malicious friend re-sends offers; the second transfer corrupts the already-filed clip.
defects.fix: Use a unique part name (`.<uuid>.part`); claim the final name atomically (`create_new`, or a move without replace, retrying on collision); reject duplicate offer ids.

defects.title: P2P fetch/serve stalls never time out; router JoinSet unbounded; outgoing secret stays valid forever
defects.claim: iroh sends a keep-alive every 5 s, so the QUIC idle timeout never fires while the peer process lives. In `fetch`, `open_bi`, `read_exact(header)` and `recv.read`, and in `serve`, `accept_bi`, `read_exact(length)` and `send.write_all` can therefore hang forever if the other side goes quiet. Cancel is only checked between chunks, so it cannot break a blocked call. The router's `JoinSet` is unbounded, so anyone who knows the NodeId can pile up idle connections. An outgoing transfer stays "Moving" with a working secret for good if the receiver disappears.
defects.scenario: The peer stops reading/writing without closing; the transfer hangs indefinitely and cannot be cancelled; or someone with the NodeId opens many idle connections that accumulate in the JoinSet.
defects.fix: Per-operation `tokio::time::timeout` (e.g. 30 s without progress); an expiry on outgoing secrets.

defects.title: Friends WebSocket connect has no timeout, freezing the reconnect loop
defects.claim: `tokio_tungstenite::connect_async` is called with no timeout; a middlebox that stalls the TLS handshake freezes the friends reconnect loop until restart.
defects.scenario: A network middlebox accepts TCP but stalls the TLS handshake; the friends connection never recovers until the app is restarted.
defects.fix: A 15 s timeout on the WebSocket connect.

defects.title: Updater builder has no timeout, so one hung check stops all hourly checks
defects.claim: The updater builder is constructed without `.timeout()`, so a single hung update check blocks and stops all subsequent hourly checks.
defects.scenario: One update request hangs on the network; the app never checks for updates again in that run.
defects.fix: Set a timeout on the updater builder.

defects.title: Share links publish the friend's name on received clips
defects.claim: Received clips are tagged `tags: vec![format!("from {from}")]` (share.rs:866). `is_friend_tag` only matches a "with " prefix, so when the user shares a received clip as a public link, the tag "from <friend's Discord display name>" goes to the public page; the server-side `cleanTags` keeps it. This contradicts the stated intent ("who played along stays among friends, a link is public"; commit f041a3d).
defects.scenario: User receives a clip from a friend, then creates a public share link for it; the public page shows "from <friend's display name>".
defects.fix: Treat "from …" as a friend tag, or better, store friend and sender tags in a structured field.

defects.title: Session token stored in plaintext in Roaming AppData
defects.claim: `std::fs::write(&path, json!({ "token": token }))` writes the bearer session token to `%APPDATA%\ClippiBoy\friends.json` in plaintext. The token stays valid for 180 days without use (renewed with use), so it follows roaming profiles and backups and any same-user malware can take it. (No token appears in the logs.)
defects.scenario: Same-user malware or anyone with access to a roaming profile/backup reads friends.json and impersonates the user to the friends server for up to 180 days.
defects.fix: Protect it with DPAPI (`CryptProtectData`) or the Windows Credential Manager (keyring), and keep it in LocalAppData.

defects.title: Any clippiboy://auth deep link consumes the pending sign-in verifier
defects.claim: `friends.verifier.lock().take()` runs before the `/auth/exchange` call, for any `clippiboy://auth?code=<junk>`. A web page (or local process) can therefore make a pending sign-in fail, and can pop error toasts when no sign-in is open. Login CSRF (victim signed into attacker's account) is blocked by PKCE unless the attacker also learns the victim's challenge (it travels in the URL query, so browser history or server logs) within 10 minutes — that part is speculative.
defects.scenario: While the user is signing in, a web page opens `clippiboy://auth?code=junk`; the verifier is taken, the real code's exchange fails. Without a sign-in in progress, the same link produces error toasts. DoS confirmed.
defects.fix: Keep the verifier until an exchange succeeds or a timeout passes; ignore links silently when no sign-in is in progress.

defects.title: P2P exposes IP addresses before accept, and friend-chosen endpoints/relays get dialled
defects.claim: The offer contains `router.endpoint().addr()`: the sender's public and LAN IPs, sent to the friend before they accept. On accept, the receiver contacts IP:ports and a relay URL chosen by the friend (iroh's `start_active_relay` ignores whether the URL is in the relay map). That reveals the receiver's IP to an attacker-run relay and sends QUIC packets to arbitrary hosts, LAN included. The privacy page doesn't say that a friend learns your public and LAN IPs (the sender's as soon as it offers), or that a friend-chosen relay host may be contacted.
defects.scenario: A malicious friend puts an attacker-run relay URL or internal LAN IP:ports in `EndpointAddr`; on accept the victim's app contacts those hosts, revealing the victim's IP and sending QUIC packets to arbitrary/LAN targets.
defects.fix: Say this in the privacy page; offer only global addresses plus the n0 relay; ignore relay URLs outside the default map; consider a relay-only option.

defects.title: Share temp tracks and crash .part files leak
defects.claim: The cut tracks in `%TEMP%\clippiboy-share\<id>\` are deleted only after a successful send (`o.tracks.drain(..)`). After Declined, Expired, Cancelled or Failed they stay forever, and nothing cleans them at startup. `.part` files from a crash stay in the user's clip folder or under `tracks\`.
defects.scenario: A share offer is declined or expires; its temp track files remain in %TEMP% indefinitely; a crash mid-receive leaves .part files in the clip folder.
defects.fix: `impl Drop` for `Outgoing` (or clean up on every end state), plus a startup sweep of those folders.

defects.title: Failed shrink leaves temp link file behind
defects.claim: In share-link creation, a failed shrink returns early via `??` and leaves `temp\link-<id>.mp4` behind.
defects.scenario: The shrink step for a share-link upload fails; the temp `link-<id>.mp4` file is never deleted.
defects.fix: Clean up on every end state (e.g. a Drop guard), plus a startup sweep of temp folders.

defects.title: safe_file_name misses Windows device names and bidi control characters
defects.claim: `safe_file_name` doesn't apply the reserved-name rules `filing::folder_name` has, so `CON.mp4` / `NUL.mp4.part` are possible: on Windows <= 10 the transfer fails or writes into a device. `COM¹`-style names aren't handled by either function. It doesn't strip Unicode format characters (`c.is_control()` misses U+202E), so a name can be shown as "…4pm.png" in Explorer, though it stays a `.mp4`.
defects.scenario: A friend offers a file named `CON.mp4` (transfer fails or writes to a device on Windows <= 10), or a name with U+202E that displays with a spoofed extension in Explorer.
defects.fix: Reuse the reserved-name logic and strip the Cf bidi characters.

defects.title: Updater downgrade through the unsigned version field in latest.json
defects.claim: The plugin's `release.version > self.current_version` comes from `latest.json`, which is unsigned; the minisign signature covers only the installer bytes. Someone with write access to the GitHub release (but without the signing key) can label an old, signed, vulnerable installer as 99.0 and it installs silently in passive mode. Nothing in the app's own code skips verification; this is a known limitation of the Tauri updater.
defects.scenario: An attacker with GitHub release write access publishes a latest.json claiming version 99.0 pointing at an old signed vulnerable installer; clients install it silently.
defects.fix: After download, check that the signature's trusted comment (`file:ClippiBoy_<ver>…`) matches `update.version`, or keep a minimum-version floor in the app.

defects.title: ffmpeg archive isn't hashed as a whole and nothing caps its size
defects.claim: The ffmpeg zip download has no size cap, and `ZipArchive` parses the unverified file; entries are copied to disk before their hash is known (only per-file SHA-256 hashes are pinned). A compromised release could fill `%LOCALAPPDATA%` (a zip bomb or an endless stream). Nothing gets executed, though.
defects.scenario: A compromised GitHub release serves an endless stream or a zip bomb; the app writes until %LOCALAPPDATA% is full.
defects.fix: Pin the zip's own SHA-256 and check it before opening; cap each entry at its expected size.

defects.title: handle_relay doesn't check that `from` is a current friend
defects.claim: `handle_relay` doesn't check that `from` is in the current friend list; it relies entirely on the server for the friendship check.
defects.scenario: A buggy or malicious server relays a message from a non-friend; the client processes it as if from a friend.
defects.fix: Check `from` against the local friend list in `handle_relay`.

defects.title: Server-supplied link.id goes into URL paths unchecked
defects.claim: `link.id` from the server goes into URL paths unchecked. A malicious server returning `../me` turns the take-down into `DELETE /me`. That only matters for the server operator, who controls the account anyway.
defects.scenario: Server returns link id `../me`; the take-down request becomes `DELETE /me`.
defects.fix: Validate/escape `link.id` before building URL paths.

defects.title: Friends outbox is an unbounded channel
defects.claim: The friends outbox is an unbounded channel, so queued outgoing messages can grow without limit.
defects.scenario: While the socket is down or slow, messages keep accumulating in memory without bound.
defects.fix: Use a bounded channel.

defects.title: Reconnect backoff has no jitter
defects.claim: The friends reconnect backoff has no jitter, so all clients come back together after a server deploy (thundering herd).
defects.scenario: After a server deploy, every client reconnects at the same backoff instants.
defects.fix: Add random jitter to the reconnect backoff.

defects.title: Unknown server messages are logged whole, up to 64 MiB
defects.claim: Unknown server messages are logged in full; with tungstenite's default 64 MiB message cap, a single message can write up to 64 MiB into the log.
defects.scenario: The server (or a bug) sends a huge unknown message; the log balloons by up to 64 MiB per message.
defects.fix: Truncate logged unknown messages.

defects.title: .expect("HTTP client") in three client builders can abort the app
defects.claim: `.expect("HTTP client")` is used in three HTTP client builders; if TLS setup ever failed it would abort the whole app, ending any recording in progress.
defects.scenario: TLS/platform verifier initialisation fails; the reqwest client build panics and the app aborts mid-recording.
defects.fix: Handle the builder error instead of panicking.

defects.title: Any Discord user can re-request friendship right after being declined, triggering an in-game banner each time
defects.claim: Any Discord user who knows a username can re-send a friend request immediately after being declined (index.ts `sendRequest`), and each request causes an in-game banner on the victim's side (friends.rs:360-366).
defects.scenario: A stranger repeatedly re-sends friend requests after each decline, popping banners during the victim's game.
defects.fix: Rate-limit or suppress re-requests after a decline.

defects.title: Unverified whether Windows toasts escape friend-supplied text in XML
defects.claim: Whether Windows toasts escape their XML (tauri-winrt-notification 0.7.3, not available locally) is unverified. The toast text comes from friends (display name, game, offer title) but only reaches a toast when banners are off.
defects.scenario: With banners off, a friend's display name/game/offer title containing XML markup is inserted into the toast XML unescaped (unverified).
defects.fix: Verify that tauri-winrt-notification escapes text, or escape it before passing.

defects.title: Privacy page says connection details of both devices pass the server; only the sender's do
defects.claim: The privacy page says "connection details of both devices" pass the server; in fact only the sender's do (in the offer). The receiver's go directly to the friend. (The page's "never reaches our server" claim is also only true while the server behaves — see NW-1.)
defects.scenario: A reader of the privacy page gets an inaccurate picture of what the server relays.
defects.fix: Correct the privacy page wording.

defects.title: Cloudflare observability logs cover /t/ping but the usage-statistics section doesn't mention it
defects.claim: "Our server does not store your IP address with it" is true for D1, but `wrangler.jsonc` has `"observability": { "enabled": true }`, so Cloudflare request logs (IP, location, time) also cover `/t/ping` for a few days. The friends section mentions Cloudflare logs; the usage-statistics section does not.
defects.scenario: A user reading the usage-statistics section believes no IP is kept for telemetry pings, while Cloudflare request logs retain it for days.
defects.fix: Mention Cloudflare request logs in the usage-statistics section (worth confirming in the dashboard).

defects.title: "Appear offline" still sends game and status to the server, not stated on the privacy page
defects.claim: With "Appear offline", the app still sends game and status to the server (kept in memory and on the socket, not passed to friends). Consistent with "friends see you as offline", but not stated on the privacy page.
defects.scenario: A user enabling "Appear offline" may assume the server no longer receives their game/status.
defects.fix: State this on the privacy page.

positives: Peer file names and game names cannot escape the clip folder: `safe_file_name` plus `filing::folder_name` strip separators, `:`, `..` and force a known extension.
The P2P transfer secret is compared in constant time.
Sign-in: the PKCE-style verifier plus the state cookie on the server are correct.
Updater: the minisign signature is checked before install; nothing in the app's own code skips verification.
ffmpeg download: each program's SHA-256 is pinned in the binary and checked before the files are moved into place; entries are read by exact name, so there is no zip-slip.
Share-link upload is streamed from disk, never whole in memory.
Server data in the WebView: no `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` anywhere; the CSP limits images to `cdn.discordapp.com`; the app never opens a URL the server sends.
control.rs (local Stream Deck port) was briefly checked and nothing was found.
No session token appears in the logs.

Telemetry: no security findings. Exactly the documented fields are sent (UUID v4, version, source, heard, three counts capped at 10,000, six feature bits); own client with no auth header and no shared connections, own thread with a 15 s timeout; nothing goes out before the notice has been seen or while the switch is off; turning it off deletes `usage.json`, turning it on again starts a new id, and a ping in flight at the switch is not recorded.
Privacy consistency: ping contents, opt-out with the notice gate, delete-on-off and new-id-on-on, and the `usage.json` path match design doc section 3.
Privacy consistency: "Without signing in, only GitHub" holds — the only hosts in the code are github.com and api.clippiboy.com (the ping); iroh starts only on the first share.
Privacy consistency: avatars come only from `cdn.discordapp.com` (enforced by the CSP).
Privacy consistency: "Show what I'm playing" and "Appear offline" behave as described.
Server relay limits are in place: 4 KB messages, 30 messages per 10 s per socket, friendship checked, `from` set by the server.
